categories.label: Linguistic and Structural Roots of Poor Readability
categories.memo: Covers text-level features—grammar, jargon, sentence structure, negative tone, and lack of visual aids—identified through NLP/DEMATEL/text-mining methods as root causes of ambiguity and misinterpretation in contract documents, distinct from broader empirical dispute causation networks.

codes.label: Grammatical Deficiencies and Sentence Structure
codes.description: Poor grammar, missing nouns, and over-shortened sentences—often resulting from simplification efforts—are identified as root causal factors of low contract readability, more significant than sentence length itself.

sub_codes.label: Missing nouns/poor grammar from over-simplification
sub_codes.description: Attempts to shorten sentences (e.g., in NEC) can strip out necessary grammatical elements, degrading clarity rather than improving it.

sub_codes.label: Sentence length as symptom not cause
sub_codes.description: Sentence length reduction, though commonly recommended, is largely an effect of deeper grammatical/terminology problems rather than an independent readability fix.

codes.label: Legal Jargon and Specialized Vocabulary
codes.description: Excessive use of legal terminology, often introduced by lawyers rather than engineers/practitioners, is a major root cause of reduced contract readability and usability.

codes.label: Ambiguous and Vague Wording
codes.description: Vagueness, abstractness, and words/sentences capable of more than one meaning are recurring linguistic sources of dispute and misinterpretation of roles and obligations.

codes.label: Scope-of-Work Complexity and Legal Term Incoherence
codes.description: Unnecessary complexity in describing scope of work, combined with controversial or incoherent use of legal terms, forms an interdependent cluster of readability risks that reinforce one another.

codes.label: Negative Language and Tone
codes.description: Negatively framed clauses can reduce trust and collaboration between parties, increasing conflict likelihood independent of technical ambiguity.

codes.label: Lack of Visual Representation
codes.description: Absence of diagrams, charts, and timelines in contract documents reduces transparency and readability, acting as a relatively independent risk factor.

codes.label: Causal Interdependency of Readability Risks
codes.description: Readability risk factors are causally interlinked (e.g., via DEMATEL analysis), meaning prioritizing surface-level fixes without addressing root causes may fail to improve clarity or reduce disputes.

categories.label: Contractual Incompleteness and Ambiguity as Dispute Drivers
categories.memo: Addresses how incomplete, ambiguous, or poorly drafted contract terms—independent of specific linguistic features—create differing interpretations of obligations and set up conditions for disputes across delivery methods.

codes.label: Incomplete or Deficient Contract Documentation
codes.description: Contract incompleteness (ambiguity, deficiency, inconsistency, defectiveness), often neglected in early project stages, is repeatedly identified as a foundational and frequent driver of construction disputes.

codes.label: Outdated Standard Contract Language
codes.description: Standard contract documents in long-term use without substantive updates may retain unfair or outdated terms that fuel disputes, indicating a need for periodic revision.

codes.label: Opportunism and Behavioral Exploitation of Ambiguity
codes.description: Incomplete or ambiguous contract terms create space for opportunistic behavior, where parties maximize self-interest by exploiting gaps or vague provisions.

codes.label: Design Documentation Ambiguity
codes.description: Missing details, ambiguous drawings, and incomplete design information—often linked to compressed design schedules—are contractual/technical triggers for disputes.

categories.label: Modification of Standard Forms and Introduced Inconsistency
categories.memo: Focuses on how amending, customizing, or reusing standard contract forms (e.g., CCDC, FIDIC, NEC)—rather than drafting anew—introduces textual inconsistency, complexity, or unbalanced risk allocation.

codes.label: Reduced Clarity from Client-Driven Modifications
codes.description: Modifications made to standard forms (typically at the client's initiative) generally reduce contract readability and clarity compared to unmodified standard text.

codes.label: Inconsistency Between Modified and Original Clauses
codes.description: Amendments and added clauses frequently create inconsistencies between clauses or across multiple contracts on a project, raising dispute potential.

codes.label: Particular Conditions as Risk-Neutral Clarification Tools
codes.description: Well-drafted particular/supplementary conditions primarily add interpretive detail and clarify obligations rather than fundamentally altering the risk-mitigation balance set by general conditions.

codes.label: Particular Conditions Increasing Complexity via Supplementation
codes.description: Particular conditions tend to increase overall contract complexity because additive (supplement) sentences outnumber deletions, especially for obligations and task descriptions.

codes.label: Risk of Over-Amending Adaptation/Contingency Clauses
codes.description: Excessive modification of clauses addressing future contingencies is riskier than amending coordination-type clauses, since future events are inherently hard to foresee; unnecessary changes should be avoided.

codes.label: Recycling Contract Templates Without Adequate Modification
codes.description: Reusing prior contract templates without proper customization for new project or delivery-method requirements is a recognized barrier that introduces ambiguity, notably relevant to standardized CCDC forms applied to non-conventional methods.

codes.label: Unilateral Drafting and Embedded Bias
codes.description: Standard forms are often drafted unilaterally by owners/clients without contractor input, and some parties deliberately insert biased or 'poisonous' clauses shifting risk, embedding textual bias into contract language.

categories.label: Automated and Computational Detection of Textual Ambiguity
categories.memo: Covers NLP, machine learning, and text-mining approaches used to detect, classify, or quantify linguistic ambiguity, risk-prone clauses, and obligation imbalance within contract text, offering tools relevant to future CCDC clause analysis.

codes.label: NLP-Based Risk Clause Detection
codes.description: Rule-based and machine-learning NLP models can detect 'poisonous' or biased clauses (e.g., in FIDIC) that unfairly favor one party, enabling proactive identification of risky language before signing.

codes.label: NLP-Based Scope and Obligation Extraction
codes.description: NLP models can automatically extract subcontractor scope and contractual obligations from design-build contract text, aiding delineation of responsibilities among disciplines.

codes.label: Machine Learning Analysis of Particular Conditions Text
codes.description: Machine learning-based coding can efficiently and objectively classify large volumes of particular-condition text, supporting firm-level knowledge management for contract drafting.

codes.label: Quantitative Risk Scoring of Contract Obligations
codes.description: Combining obligation extraction with risk scoring reveals which contractual commitments pose the greatest threat to project objectives, enabling prioritized monitoring of high-risk clauses.

codes.label: Text-Mining of Legal Case Data
codes.description: Analysis of litigation/defect case text can reveal recurring contractual and drafting failures, informing prevention strategies for future contract language.

categories.label: Delivery-Method-Specific Textual Gaps (MMC/Modular)
categories.memo: Addresses how existing standard contract language and definitions fail to adequately capture the realities of modern methods of construction and prefabrication, creating ambiguity specific to off-site/modular delivery.

codes.label: Absence of Standard MOC-Specific Contracts
codes.description: No standard contracts exist for modular/off-site construction in Canada, forcing adaptation of conventional-construction-based standard forms, which increases textual ambiguity and dispute potential.

codes.label: Ambiguous Definitions Failing to Capture Prefabrication
codes.description: Key contractual definitions (e.g., 'Products', payment/completion clauses) are drafted around on-site conventional construction and do not clearly encompass prefabricated modules or off-site production processes.

codes.label: Insufficient Specifications for Modular/Off-Site Work
codes.description: Standard contract specifications lack adequate, separate provisions for modular and off-site construction compared to conventional construction, contributing to textual ambiguity and dispute risk.

codes.label: Gap Between Literature-Identified and Litigated Textual Risks
codes.description: Ambiguities emphasized in MMC/modular literature (e.g., transportation regulation conflicts, local industry readiness) often do not correspond to issues actually litigated, revealing a mismatch between anticipated and observed contractual ambiguity.
